about: Model entries for docs/SRI-RUDRAM-BRIEF.md. Match their depth, tone and format. They are copied into N01.json and C01.json by the writers of those anuvākas.

title.en: Homage to the wrath and the weapons; Rudra asked to be gentle

N1.summary: Fifteen ṛks. The worshipper salutes Rudra’s wrath, arrow, bow and arms, asks that his arrow, bow and body be auspicious (śiva) and not harm people or cattle, praises the red-brown Rudra who is seen even by cowherds and water-carriers, and ends by asking him to unstring his bow and lay his weapons away from us. Sāyaṇa reads every salutation as a plea that the weapon turn on the worshipper’s enemies and not on him.

words.meaning: to the wrath, to the anger

words.gram: verb, root as (2nd class, P.), imperative 3rd sg. active
words.meaning: let it be, may it be

sandhi.rule: visarga before t becomes s (visarjanīyasya saḥ, P. 8.3.34)
final e before a vowel becomes ay (P. 6.1.78), and the y is dropped (P. 8.3.19), leaving the hiatus a u
as manyava uta: te before a vowel becomes ta

vyakarana.note: The dative goes with namaḥ: ‘homage to X’ takes the dative (namaḥsvasti…, P. 2.3.16). So do iṣave, dhanvane, bāhubhyām.
The enclitic te (for tava, ‘your’; P. 8.1.22) never stands first in its clause; here it depends on manyave.
Imperative of as ‘to be’. In the first and third clauses the verb is understood; namaḥ is the subject: ‘homage be’.

translation.literal: Homage to your wrath, O Rudra, and also to your arrow homage. Homage be to your bow, and to your two arms homage.
translation.readable: O Rudra, homage to your wrath, and homage to your arrow; homage to your bow, and homage to your two arms.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa glosses manyu as anger (कोपः) and reads the salutation as a plea about where that anger should go: «स मन्युरस्मद्वैरिष्वेव प्रसरतु नत्वस्मासु» — may it spread among our enemies, not among us. The arrow, the bow and the arms that hold them are saluted in the same spirit: «न तु मयीत्यभिप्रायः», ‘the sense is: not against me’. The Kalpa he quotes uses these anuvākas for the Śatarudrīya offering at the building of the fire altar.
units.reflection: The hymn opens by bowing to the very things one fears — wrath, arrow, bow, arm — before asking for anything. Homage here is a way of facing what threatens.

words.gram: adj. f. nom. sg., superlative of śiva
verb, causative stem mṛḍaya-, imperative 2nd sg. active

sandhi.rule: te before a vowel becomes ta
visarga before ś becomes ś (doubled sibilant, as the Taittirīya text writes it; P. 8.3.36 allows visarga or the sibilant)
final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra, written as the nasal of the next consonant’s class (m before b; P. 8.3.23, 8.4.59)

vyakarana.note: śiva + the superlative suffix -tama (P. 5.3.55), feminine to agree with iṣuḥ.
Perfect of bhū. With śivam … dhanuḥ: ‘your bow has become kindly’ — said as an appeal that it be so.
Picks up all three: the arrow, the bow and the quiver (Sāyaṇa takes tayā with each).

translation.literal: Your arrow which is most kindly, your bow which has become kindly, your missile which is kindly — with that, O Rudra, be gracious to us.
translation.readable: O Rudra, with your arrow made most kindly, your bow made kindly and your quiver made kindly, be gracious to us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads śiva here as शान्त, calm or appeased: the arrow is शान्ततमा, the bow शान्तं. He takes śaravyā as the quiver (तवेषुधिः) and mṛḍaya as सुखय, ‘make happy’. Their calm, he says, is because they do not move against devotees: «भक्तेषु प्रवृत्त्यभावात्तेषां शान्तत्वम्».

flags.note: śaravyā is ‘missile, arrow-shot’ in the dictionaries; Sāyaṇa takes it as the quiver. The translation follows Sāyaṇa and the word table gives both.

words.context: joins each item to the list (Sāyaṇa: समुच्चयार्थः)
with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’

sandhi.rule: visarga before c becomes ś (P. 8.3.34, 8.4.40); so throughout: -aś ca, -iś ca, -uś ca

vyakarana.note: Enclitic me (for mama / mahyam, P. 8.1.22). The verb is not in this anuvāka: Sāyaṇa supplies कल्पताम् from anuvāka 10 to every item — ‘may [food] be ready for me’.
Every item is followed by ca me; the refrain is part of the text, not an abbreviation, and is recited with each item.

translation.literal: Food and for me, impulse and for me, effort and for me, continuance and for me, thought and for me, resolve and for me, sound and for me, hymn and for me, hearing and for me, what is heard and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May food be mine, and the impulse to act, and effort, and its continuance; may thought be mine, and resolve, and voice, and the hymn, and the power to hear and what is heard.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «वाजोऽन्नम्» — vāja is food. The word ca joins each item to the list (समुच्चयार्थः). मे means मम, ‘mine’, and the verb comes from the tenth anuvāka: «मे मम कल्पतामिति पदं दशमानुवाके वक्ष्यमाणं सर्वत्रानुषज्यते संपद्यतामित्यर्थः» — ‘may it be accomplished for me’.
